items.title: [Bug]: Desktop multi-window on different gateways mixes session/pin lists after update

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
### Bug Description

Two Hermes Desktop windows on the same macOS machine — window A connected to the LOCAL gateway, window B to a REMOTE gateway (VPS) — each showed its own gateway sessions correctly until today's app update. After the update the two windows' sidebar session lists are mixed:

- Left window (local): 10 pinned sessions with letter badges (D/K) and a Kanban nav item.
- Right window (remote): a different but OVERLAPPING PINNED list (6 items — a subset of the left window's pins), a different SESSIONS section (4 items), NO Kanban nav item, and a green status dot on one item.

Pin/session state from one connection is bleeding into the other window's sidebar. No gateway identity is visible anywhere (no title text, no endpoint label), so the only way to tell which gateway a window is on is the manually-applied theme color.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Launch Hermes Desktop on macOS and open a second window (two HDA windows, one app process — primary + secondary).
2. Connect window A to the LOCAL gateway; connect window B to a REMOTE gateway (Settings → Gateway, remote endpoint on a VPS).
3. Pin several sessions in each window (pins reconcile against each gateway's own state.db).
4. Update the desktop app (2026-07-30 build, v0.19.1), quit, relaunch, reopen both windows.
5. Compare the two sidebars: PINNED and SESSIONS lists are mixed/overlapping — pins from one gateway appear in the other window, and the SESSIONS sections don't match each gateway's own list.
6. Note also: Kanban nav appears in only one window, and no gateway identity text exists in either titlebar.

### Expected Behavior

Each window shows only the sessions and pins of the gateway it is connected to. Window state (pinned set, session list cache, nav) is isolated per connection; one window's connection/reconcile must never mutate the other window's view.

### Actual Behavior

Pin/session state is shared or cross-reconciled between windows on different gateways: the PINNED lists overlap across the two windows (one is a subset of the other), SESSIONS sections differ from each gateway's actual list, and per-window nav differs (Kanban present in one window only). No gateway identity is displayed anywhere, so the only differentiator is the manually applied theme color.

### Affected Component

Other

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only)

### Debug Report

```shell
https://support.nousresearch.com/diagnostics/4dc4f861-a843-467c-84db-f511a826f9b1 (Nous-private diagnostic bundle, 14-day expiry; uploaded via `hermes debug share -y --nous`)
```

### Operating System

macOS 26.5.2

### Python Version

_No response_

### Hermes Version

Hermes Agent v0.19.1 (2026.7.30)

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell
OS: macOS 26.5.2 (Mac mini)
Hermes: Hermes Agent v0.19.1 (2026.7.30) · upstream d79a6f0e · local aac74be2 · install method: git
Python: 3.x (system)
Screenshot: two-window sidebar comparison — left 10 pinned + Kanban nav; right 6 overlapping pins, different SESSIONS list, no Kanban.
```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

apps/desktop/src/store/session-pin-sync.ts reconciles the sidebar pin set in PROCESS-GLOBAL module state (module-level `mirrored` / `pending` / `unconfirmed` Sets) against ONE shared localStorage pin store ($pinnedSessionIds), while the app supports multiple BrowserWindows each connected to a DIFFERENT gateway (primary + per-session secondary windows, hermes:window:openSession). With two windows reconciling against two gateways:

- pullRemotePins() adopts server pin state for every row in the current page — window B's page reads can adopt/drop pins belonging to window A's gateway and vice-versa (the observed subset overlap).
- Module-level singletons are shared across windows in the same process, so a PATCH from one window can be mirrored into the other window's store.

Also, the AGENTS.md "soft re-home" contract says a connection/mode apply must explicitly WIPE gateway-bound stores before reconnect ("Query invalidation alone cannot evict live session stores — wipe them"). A regression there would leave stale rows from the other connection's session list.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

1. Scope pin-sync state and the localStorage pin store per connection identity (gateway baseUrl/profile), not globally.
2. On connection apply, wipe gateway-bound stores (sessions, pins, caches) per window, per the soft re-home contract.
3. Bonus: surface the active gateway endpoint (host/IP) in each window's titlebar so multi-gateway users can identify windows at a glance.

Local workaround shipped meanwhile: a desktop plugin (gateway-badge, ~/.hermes/desktop-plugins/gateway-badge/plugin.js) renders the connected gateway host in titleBar.center via window.hermesDesktop.getConnection(profile) and mirrors it into document.title — identification only, does not fix the mixing.

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [ ] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: [Bug]: WebUI user messages lose workspace prefix on replay, nuking prompt cache every turn

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: P0
labels.description: Critical — data loss, security, crash loop

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

labels.name: sweeper:risk-caching
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break/degrade prompt caching or cache-key stability (invariant)

items.body:
# `api_content` sidecar not substituted for historical user messages in the main-loop api_messages build — WebUI sessions re-prefill the full context on every new user turn

## Summary

In the WebUI, every user message is sent to the model prefixed with the workspace sentinel (`[Workspace::v1: /path]\n`) while the persisted `content` column stores the bare text. The exact sent bytes are preserved in the `api_content` sidecar ("persist-what-you-send"). The main-loop api_messages build in `agent/conversation_loop.py` pops that sidecar from **every** message but substitutes it into `content` **only for the current turn's user message** (`idx == current_turn_user_idx`). Historical user messages are therefore re-sent without the workspace prefix on turn 2+, which diverges from the bytes the server cached on turn 1 — so the provider prompt-cache prefix breaks at the first conversation message and the **entire context re-prefills at the start of every new user turn**.

On local OpenAI-compatible backends (llama.cpp / LM Studio / vLLM) this is a multi-minute stall: a 90K-token context re-prefills in ~2–4 minutes before the model answers a one-line follow-up. On cloud providers it is an invisible per-turn cache-miss billing drip.

## Environment

- Hermes Agent 0.19.1 (verified 2026-08-03), WebUI surface (two-container deployment: `hermes-webui` + `hermes-agent`)
- Local backend: llama.cpp server via llama-swap (Qwen3.6-27B, single slot, `--cache-ram` + ctx checkpoints)
- Cache reuse measured via `usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens` on every API call

## Reproduction

1. Start a WebUI session with a local OpenAI-compatible backend.
2. Turn 1: any normal query (tool-using or not). Let it complete.
3. Turn 2: any one-line follow-up.
4. Observe turn 2's **first** API call.

**Actual:** `cached_tokens` falls back to the system+tools header only (~22,317 tokens in a default WebUI session) — the whole conversation after the first user message re-prefills. Every subsequent call in turn 2 is then warm again (96–100%), and the pattern repeats on every new turn.

Real session log (user session `cb8c904c3430`, turn 2 = "Weather tomorrow?", turn 3 = "NYC"):

```
API call #4: in=27589 cache=26060/27589 (94%)   <- end of turn 1 (warm)
API call #5: in=27775 cache=22317/27775 (80%)   <- turn 2 FIRST call: header-only
API call #6: in=29063 cache=27903/29063 (96%)   <- recovers within turn 2
API call #7: in=29225 cache=22317/29225 (76%)   <- turn 3 FIRST call: header-only again
API call #8: in=30145 cache=29280/30145 (97%)   <- recovers within turn 3
```

`22317` is the byte-stable system+tools header: the cached prefix matches up to the first conversation message and diverges exactly there. With a 90K context, the re-prefill at turn 2 is ~68K tokens — the user canceled a follow-up after 15s of silence (`stream_interrupt_abort`, `reason=interrupted_during_api_call`) in a session that had been running at 96–100% cache a minute earlier.

**Expected:** `cached_tokens ≈` previous request's total (a byte-stable append; only the new user message is new).

## Root cause

The WebUI sends user messages prefixed with `[Workspace::v1: /path]\n` (`api/streaming.py::_workspace_context_prefix`) and stores:
- `content` = bare text (`'What's my most recent email'`)
- `api_content` = exact sent bytes (`'[Workspace::v1: /workspace]\nWhat's my most recent email'`)

On reload, `get_messages_as_conversation` returns the message with `content` bare and `api_content` present. The main-loop build then:

```python
# agent/conversation_loop.py (api_messages build, ~lines 1574-1611)
for idx, msg in enumerate(messages):
    api_msg = msg.copy()
    _api_content = api_msg.pop("api_content", None)   # popped from EVERY message
    ...
    # Inject ephemeral context into the current turn's user message.
    if idx == current_turn_user_idx and msg.get("role") == "user":
        if isinstance(_api_content, str) and _api_content:
            api_msg["content"] = _api_content          # substituted ONLY here
        else:
            _composed = compose_user_api_content(...)  # ephemeral injection
```

Historical user messages (and any assistant message carrying a sidecar) get their sidecar **popped and discarded** — the bare `content` goes to the provider. The server had cached the prefixed bytes; the re-render now lacks the prefix → divergence at the first historical user message → header-only cache.

**The same mechanism is correctly implemented in the summary path** (`agent/chat_completion_helpers.py:2134`), whose comment states the intent explicitly:

```python
# api_content (the persist-what-you-send sidecar) carries the
# exact bytes every main-loop call sent for this message —
# substitute it before dropping the key ... Popping without
# substituting would send CLEAN content here, diverging the
# summary request's prefix at the EARLIEST sidecar-carrying
# message and re-prefilling the whole transcript at exactly
# the moment the context is largest.
substitute_api_content(api_msg)
```

`agent/turn_context.py::substitute_api_content`'s own docstring claims it is "Used at every API-bound message-build site (the api_messages build in `conversation_loop`, the max-iterations summary in `chat_completion_helpers`, the chat-completions transport)". A repo-wide grep shows **one call site** — the summary path only. The main-loop call is missing (regression or the docstring is aspirational). The chat-completions transport (`agent/transports/chat_completions.py:241`) also only pops the sidecar, never substitutes.

## Why the CLI cannot reproduce this

The CLI path has no workspace prefix at all — `content` is consistently bare, so nothing ever diverges. That is why the symptom is WebUI-only and why it is easy to miss. Reproduced deliberately by injecting the exact WebUI storage shape into a CLI session (bare `content` + prefixed `api_content` sidecar):

```
WITH the fix:    turn 2 first call: in=21907 cache=21891/21907 (100%)
WITHOUT the fix: turn 2 first call: header-only match (the conversation re-prefills)
```

## Measured impact

| Scenario | Cache on turn-2 first call | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| Within turn 1 (any call 2+) | 96–100% | none |
| Turn 2 first call (WebUI, current code) | header-only (~22K of 90K) | ~68K-token re-prefill, ~2–4 min on local |
| Turn 2 first call with sidecar substitution | ~100% | only the new user message |

Cloud providers are affected invisibly: the same byte divergence breaks content-addressed cache prefixes on every new turn (billing drip, higher TTFT).

## Suggested fix

In the main-loop api_messages build (`conversation_loop.py`), substitute the sidecar for **every** user/assistant message that carries it, not only the current turn — preserving the current-turn ephemeral-injection branch:

```python
_api_content = api_msg.pop("api_content", None)
if (
    idx != current_turn_user_idx
    and isinstance(_api_content, str)
    and _api_content
    and msg.get("role") in ("user", "assistant")
):
    api_msg["content"] = _api_content
```

This mirrors the summary path and makes the docstring true.

items.title: [Feature Proposal] Adopting Advanced Tooling Patterns from Oh My Pi — Hashline Edits, LSP/DAP Integration, AST Tools, and More
items.body:
## Summary

This proposal recommends adopting several proven tooling patterns from [Oh My Pi](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi) (OMP) into Hermes Agent. OMP demonstrated that **harness-level improvements can boost LLM coding performance by 5-64 points across 16 models** with zero training compute — just by changing how tools present themselves to the model.

Hermes already has a strong foundation (multi-platform gateway, skills, memory, delegation). These additions would make it significantly more powerful as a **coding agent** while maintaining the general-purpose architecture.

---

## 1. Hashline Edit Tool (Priority: High)

### Problem

Current edit tools (str_replace, apply_patch, fuzzy replace) rely on the model reproducing exact text content. This causes:
- High failure rates when whitespace/indentation differs
- Retry loops wasting tokens
- Models penalized for mechanical failures, not reasoning failures

### Proposal

Adopt OMP's **hashline** approach: each line gets a 2-3 character content hash when read. The model references hashes instead of reproducing text.

```
1:a3|function hello() {
2:f1|  return "world";
3:0e|}
```

Edit command: `replace line 2:f1`, `replace range 1:a3 through 3:0e`

### Impact (from OMP benchmarks)

- Grok Code Fast 1: 6.7% → 68.3% (10x improvement)
- MiniMax: 2.1x pass rate improvement
- Grok 4 Fast: -61% output tokens (no more retry loops)
- Gemini 3 Flash: +5pp over str_replace
- Average: +15pts across 16 models

### Implementation Notes

- Modify `read_file` / `search_files` to include line hashes
- New `edit` tool variant that accepts hash references
- Stale anchor detection (file changed since last read → reject edit)
- Keep existing edit tools as fallback

---

## 2. LSP Integration (Priority: High)

### Problem

Hermes can read/write files but lacks IDE-level code intelligence. Operations like rename, find references, go-to-definition require manual text search.

### Proposal

Integrate Language Server Protocol (LSP) as a tool with operations:
- `lsp diagnostics` — get errors/warnings
- `lsp references` — find all references to a symbol
- `lsp rename` — rename across all files (with import updates)
- `lsp definition` — go to definition
- `lsp code_actions` — refactoring suggestions
- `lsp symbols` — outline of current file

### Implementation Notes

- Use existing LSP servers (pyright, typescript-language-server, rust-analyzer, etc.)
- Lazy-start LSP servers on first use
- Cache diagnostics per file
- Return structured results, not raw JSON

---

## 3. DAP (Debug Adapter Protocol) Integration (Priority: Medium)

### Problem

Debugging currently requires manual print statements or attaching debuggers externally.

### Proposal

Drive debug sessions through DAP:
- Set/remove breakpoints
- Step over/into/out
- Inspect variables at any scope
- Evaluate expressions
- List threads and stack frames

### Supported Adapters

- debugpy (Python)
- lldb-dap (C/C++/Rust)
- dlv (Go)
- Node inspector (JavaScript/TypeScript)

---

## 4. AST-Based Tools (Priority: Medium)

### Problem

Regex-based search/edit fails on structural code changes (rename a function across complex expressions).

### Proposal

Add AST-aware tools:
- `ast_grep` — structural code queries over 50+ tree-sitter grammars
- `ast_edit` — structural rewrites with preview before apply

### Use Cases

- "Find all function calls to `formatBytes` and rename to `formatSize`"
- "Remove all `console.log` statements from this file"
- "Add error handling around every `fetch()` call"

---

## 5. Code Execution with Tool Loopback (Priority: Medium)

### Problem

Current `execute_code` runs Python in isolation. It cannot call back into Hermes tools.

### Proposal

Persistent Python/Bun/Ruby/Julia kernels that can call Hermes tools via loopback:
- Agent reads CSV with `tool.read` from inside Python
- Charts data from JavaScript
- Never leaves the cell

### Implementation Notes

- Persistent kernel sessions (not one-shot)
- Loopback bridge: `hermes.tool_call(name, args)` from kernel
- Kernel state persists across calls in same session

---

## 6. Time-Traveling Stream Rules (Priority: Low)

### Problem

Agent rules/guidelines are injected once at system prompt. Violations require full context re-injection.

### Proposal

Regex-based stream monitoring:
- Match pattern in agent output → abort stream mid-token
- Inject rule as system reminder
- Retry from same position
- Rules survive compaction

### Use Cases

- Catch forbidden patterns (e.g., `Box::leak` in production code)
- Enforce style rules in real-time
- Auto-correct before response completes

---

## 7. Advisor Model (Priority: Low)

### Proposal

Pair a second model to "advisor" role:
- Reads every turn the main agent takes
- Injects inline notes (concern, suggestion, hard blocker)
- Runs on own context and model
- Main agent sees note and course-corrects

### Use Cases

- Security review on every code change
- Architecture compliance checking
- Second opinion on critical decisions

---

## 8. Enhanced Subagent Coordination (Priority: Medium)

### Current State

`delegate_task` works but lacks:
- Live transcript streaming ✅ (done in v0.19.0)
- Typed schema-validated results
- Workspace isolation (worktrees)

### Proposal

- Schema-validated yield results
- Git worktree isolation for parallel coding
- Subagent-to-subagent communication

---

## 9. Collab Sessions (Priority: Low)

### Proposal

Real-time collaborative sessions:
- `/collab` generates shareable link + QR
- Read-write or view-only modes
- WebRTC or relay-based
- End-to-end encrypted frames

---

## 10. Observability Dashboard (Priority: Low)

### Proposal

Local observability dashboard:
- Token usage per session/model
- Tool call statistics
- Cost tracking
- Performance metrics
- Export for analysis

---

## Priority Summary

| Priority | Feature | Impact | Effort |
|----------|---------|--------|--------|
| High | Hashline Edits | Very High | Medium |
| High | LSP Integration | High | Medium |
| Medium | DAP Integration | Medium | High |
| Medium | AST Tools | Medium | Medium |
| Medium | Code Execution Loopback | Medium | Medium |
| Medium | Enhanced Subagents | Medium | Low (partially done) |
| Low | Time-Traveling Rules | Low | Low |
| Low | Advisor Model | Low | Medium |
| Low | Collab Sessions | Low | High |
| Low | Observability Dashboard | Low | Medium |

---

## References

- [OMP Blog: The Harness Problem](https://blog.can.ac/2026/02/12/the-harness-problem/) — benchmark data showing harness impact
- [OMP Edit Tool Source](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/blob/main/packages/coding-agent/src/tools/index.ts)
- [OMP Hashline Package](https://github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi/tree/main/packages/hashline)

---

## Notes

This proposal is from a Hermes Agent user who compared both systems. The goal is not to make Hermes a clone of OMP, but to **adopt proven patterns** that would make Hermes significantly stronger as a coding agent while maintaining its multi-platform, general-purpose architecture.

Hermes already excels at: multi-platform messaging, skills system, memory, delegation, cron, web automation. Adding these coding-specific tools would make it a complete solution.

items.title: [Feature Proposal] LSP/DAP Integration, AST Tools, and Targeted Gaps from Oh My Pi Analysis
items.body:
## Context

After deep-diving into both codebases (Hermes Agent v0.19.1 installed at `/usr/local/lib/hermes-agent/` and Oh My Pi source at `github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi`), this proposal focuses on **actual gaps** — features OMP has that Hermes genuinely lacks, not things Hermes already does differently but well.

### What Hermes Already Has (and does well)

| Capability | Hermes Implementation | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Edit tool | `patch` (V4A format) + `fuzzy_match.py` (9-strategy chain) | 1108 lines of fuzzy matching. Handles whitespace, indentation, unicode normalization. Different from hashline but proven. |
| Code execution loopback | `code_execution_tool.py` — UDS RPC + file-based RPC | 2087 lines. Already supports 7 tools inside sandbox (`web_search`, `read_file`, `write_file`, `search_files`, `patch`, `terminal`, `web_extract`). Loopback bridge exists. |
| Subagent delegation | `delegate_tool.py` — ThreadPoolExecutor, blocked tools, approval | 3974 lines. Live transcripts (v0.19.0). Schema validation exists. |
| Memory | `memory_tool.py` — file-backed MEMORY.md + USER.md | Frozen snapshot in system prompt, mid-session writes don't invalidate cache. |
| Skills | `skills_tool.py` + `skill_manager_tool.py` | Procedural memory, auto-learn, Skills Hub. |
| Browser | `browser_tool.py` + CDP | Puppeteer/CDP-based browser automation. |
| Computer Use | `computer_use/` — CUA driver | Desktop automation with background delivery. |
| MCP | `mcp_tool.py` + `mcp_stdio_watchdog.py` | Full MCP server integration. |
| Multi-platform | Gateway — Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, etc. | 20+ platforms from one gateway. |

### What Oh My Pi Has That Hermes Genuinely Lacks

| Feature | OMP Implementation | Hermes Gap |
|---|---|---|
| **LSP integration** | 14 operations — diagnostics, references, rename, definition, code actions, symbols | **No LSP at all.** Hermes does text-based search/replace. Rename across files requires manual grep. |
| **DAP integration** | 28 operations — breakpoints, stepping, threads, variables, evaluate | **No debugger driving.** Hermes can run code but can't attach and step through it. |
| **AST-based tools** | `ast_grep` (tree-sitter 50+ grammars) + `ast_edit` (structural rewrites with preview) | **No AST awareness.** `grep` is regex-only. Structural refactoring (rename function across expressions) is manual. |
| **Hashline edits** | Content-hash anchors per line, stale-anchor rejection | Hermes has fuzzy matching (different approach). Hashline's advantage: model references 2-3 char tags instead of reproducing text. Benchmark: +15pts avg across 16 models. |
| **Time-traveling stream rules** | Regex match → abort stream → inject rule → retry from same point | **No stream monitoring.** Rules are static in system prompt. No mid-stream correction. |
| **Advisor model** | Second model reads every turn, injects inline notes | **No dual-model review.** Hermes has approval system but not a continuous model-level reviewer. |
| **Collab sessions** | `/collab` → shareable link + QR, read-write or view-only | **No real-time collab.** Sessions are single-user. |
| **Observability dashboard** | `omp-stats` — local token/cost/perf tracking | Hermes has logs but no structured dashboard. |

---

## Proposal: Targeted Improvements

### 1. LSP Integration Tool (Priority: High)

**Why:** This is the single biggest gap. LSP gives the agent IDE-level intelligence — rename across all files with import updates, find all references, go-to-definition, diagnostics. Currently Hermes relies on text search which misses semantic relationships.

**Implementation approach:**
- New tool: `lsp` with sub-operations (diagnostics, references, rename, definition, code_actions, symbols)
- Lazy-start LSP servers: spawn `pyright`, `typescript-language-server`, `rust-analyzer` on first use per workspace
- Use existing LSP implementations (Node.js `vscode-languageserver-protocol` or Python `lsprotocol`)
- Return structured results, not raw JSON
- Cache diagnostics per file, invalidate on write

**Key difference from OMP:** OMP's LSP is tightly integrated into the agent loop. Hermes should make it a standalone tool that agents can call explicitly, keeping the architecture modular.

---

### 2. AST-Based Tools (Priority: High)

**Why:** Regex search/edit fails on structural code changes. "Rename function `formatBytes` to `formatSize`" requires understanding syntax, not just text patterns.

**Implementation approach:**
- New tool: `ast_grep` — structural code queries using tree-sitter grammars
- New tool: `ast_edit` — structural rewrites with preview before apply
- Use `tree-sitter` bindings (Python: `tree_sitter`, or shell out to `ast-grep` CLI)
- Support top 10 languages initially (Python, JS/TS, Rust, Go, Java, C/C++, Ruby, PHP, Swift, Kotlin)
- Auto-include when `grep`/`patch` are active (matching OMP's behavior)

**Key difference from OMP:** OMP bundles tree-sitter as Rust N-API bindings. Hermes could use the `tree-sitter` Python package or the `ast-grep` CLI tool for simpler integration.

---

### 3. DAP (Debug Adapter Protocol) Integration (Priority: Medium)

**Why:** Hermes can run code but can't drive a debugger. For complex bugs, the agent needs to set breakpoints, step through code, inspect variables.

**Implementation approach:**
- New tool: `debug` with operations (set_breakpoint, step_over, step_into, step_out, continue, inspect_variables, evaluate_expression, list_threads, list_stack_frames)
- Use DAP client library (Python: `debugpy` for Python, or raw DAP protocol over stdio)
- Start with Python (debugpy) and Node.js (inspector) support
- Lazy-start debug adapter on first use

**Key difference from OMP:** OMP supports 4 adapters (debugpy, lldb-dap, dlv, node). Hermes should start with 2 (debugpy + node inspector) and expand.

---

### 4. Hashline Edit as Alternative Mode (Priority: Medium)

**Why:** OMP's benchmarks show hashline beats fuzzy matching on average (+15pts across 16 models). Not a replacement for Hermes' fuzzy matching, but an alternative mode.

**Implementation approach:**
- Add hashline mode to existing `patch` tool (new `mode: "hashline"`)
- When `read_file` returns content, include 2-3 char content hashes per line
- Agent references hashes in edit commands: `replace line 2:f1`, `replace range 1:a3 through 3:0e`
- Stale anchor detection: if file changed since last read, hashes don't match → reject
- Keep existing fuzzy matching as default, hashline as opt-in

**Key difference from OMP:** Hermes keeps its proven fuzzy matching as default. Hashline becomes an alternative that models can opt into.

---

### 5. Time-Traveling Stream Rules (Priority: Low)

**Why:** Currently rules are static in system prompt. If the model violates a rule, the violation completes before the agent can correct it.

**Implementation approach:**
- Regex-based stream monitoring in the agent loop
- When pattern matches in agent output: abort stream mid-token, inject rule as system reminder, retry from same position
- Rules configurable per session/project
- Rules survive context compaction

**Key difference from OMP:** OMP's implementation is tightly coupled to its TypeScript agent loop. Hermes' implementation should be a middleware/hook in the existing agent pipeline.

---

### 6. Advisor Model (Priority: Low)

**Why:** A second model reviewing every turn catches things the primary model misses — security issues, architecture violations, edge cases.

**Implementation approach:**
- New config: `advisor.model` — model used for review
- New config: `advisor.mode` — "inline" (inject notes into conversation) or "shadow" (log only)
- Advisor runs on its own context, reads every turn
- Injects notes as system reminders: concern, suggestion, or hard blocker
- Main agent sees note and can course-correct

**Key difference from OMP:** OMP's advisor is always-on. Hermes should make it opt-in and configurable per session.

---

### 7. Enhanced `execute_code` Sandbox Tools (Priority: Low)

**Why:** Hermes' sandbox already supports 7 tools. OMP's eval supports more (read, write, search, task). Expanding the sandbox tool set would make code execution more powerful.

**Current Hermes sandbox tools:**
```python
SANDBOX_ALLOWED_TOOLS = frozenset([
    "web_search", "web_extract", "read_file", "write_file",
    "search_files", "patch", "terminal",
])
```

**Proposal:** Add `delegate_task`, `memory`, `skills_list`, `skill_view` to sandbox. This lets Python scripts inside the sandbox orchestrate subagents, access memory, and use skills.

---

## Priority Summary

| Priority | Feature | Impact | Effort | Already in Hermes? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| High | LSP Integration | Very High | Medium | No |
| High | AST-Based Tools | High | Medium | No |
| Medium | DAP Integration | Medium | High | No |
| Medium | Hashline Edit Mode | Medium | Low | No (different approach exists) |
| Low | Time-Traveling Rules | Low | Low | No |
| Low | Advisor Model | Low | Medium | No |
| Low | Expand Sandbox Tools | Low | Low | Partially (7 tools exist) |

---

## What NOT to Propose (Hermes Already Does Well)

- **Fuzzy matching** — Hermes' 9-strategy chain is more robust than OMP's hashline for whitespace/indentation issues. Don't replace, offer as alternative.
- **Code execution loopback** — Already exists via UDS RPC. Just needs more tools exposed.
- **Subagent delegation** — Already works with live transcripts. Schema validation exists.
- **Memory system** — File-backed with frozen snapshot. Different from OMP's SQLite but proven.
- **Skills system** — More mature than OMP's. Auto-learn, Skills Hub, provenance tracking.
- **Multi-platform gateway** — OMP is terminal-only. Hermes supports 20+ platforms.
- **Browser automation** — Both have it. Hermes' CDP implementation is solid.
- **MCP integration** — Both have it. Hermes has MCP dashboard and OAuth.

---

## References

- Hermes source: `/usr/local/lib/hermes-agent/` (v0.19.1)
  - `tools/patch_parser.py` — V4A patch format (693 lines)
  - `tools/fuzzy_match.py` — 9-strategy fuzzy matching (1108 lines)
  - `tools/code_execution_tool.py` — PTC with UDS RPC loopback (2087 lines)
  - `tools/delegate_tool.py` — Subagent architecture (3974 lines)
  - `tools/memory_tool.py` — Persistent memory (1240 lines)
  - `tools/file_tools.py` — File operations (2319 lines)
- OMP source: `github.com/can1357/oh-my-pi`
  - `packages/hashline/` — Hashline edit algorithm
  - `packages/coding-agent/src/tools/` — All 32 built-in tools
  - `packages/mnemopi/` — SQLite memory engine
  - `packages/agent/` — Agent loop with stream monitoring
- OMP benchmarks: `blog.can.ac/2026/02/12/the-harness-problem/`

---

## Notes

This is a revised proposal after deep analysis of both codebases. The original proposal included features Hermes already has (code execution loopback, subagent delegation, memory). This version focuses on **actual gaps** where OMP has capabilities Hermes genuinely lacks.

The goal remains: adopt proven patterns that make Hermes stronger as a coding agent while maintaining its multi-platform, general-purpose architecture.

items.title: 5s compression busy-wait (#75264) is an order of magnitude shorter than real LLM compressions — turns still die as session_persistence_failed with a misleading "Disk full" dialog

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
### Environment

- Hermes Agent 0.19.1, `main` @ `a4a91610b0` (includes #75264)
- macOS (Darwin 25.2), native gateway (no Docker), desktop app + background workers
- State DB on a healthy volume with 85 GB free — nothing is actually full

### Summary

#75083 was fixed in #75264 by briefly waiting out a live compression lock before failing `append_message`. That fix works for the case it assumed — the code comment says *"Compression publishes in a couple of seconds, so a brief wait saves the overwhelming majority of concurrent turns"* — and sets `_COMPRESSION_BUSY_WAIT_S = 5.0`.

But LLM-streamed context compression routinely takes **minutes, not seconds**. In the incident below, two consecutive compressions took **129s and 148s** (the compression path itself logs *"still streaming after 120s — extending wait (ceiling 600s)"*, i.e. it expects to run up to 10 minutes). A 5s busy-wait against a 2.5-minute lock loses every time, so every turn that writes during a compression window still dies as `session_persistence_failed`, and the user still gets the misleading disk-space toast that #75083 was raised about:

> ⚠️ No reply: the turn was stopped because session storage could not be written (the transcript would have been lost on restart). This is often a full disk — free some space (or fix state.db permissions), then send your message again.

The desktop surfaces this as a **"Disk full — free some space, then try again"** dialog even though `is_disk_full_error()` is (correctly) false for `SessionCompressionInProgressError` — the reason-string mapping in the desktop/turn-summary path doesn't distinguish the lock case.

### Aggravating loop

A session sitting right at the compression threshold makes this near-deterministic rather than a rare race:

1. Session is at ~231.5k tokens; threshold for the active model is 231.2k → **every prompt** triggers pre-API compression.
2. Compression streams for 2+ minutes holding the lock.
3. Any turn activity during that window fails `append_message` after the 5s wait → turn destroyed → toast.
4. User retries (or a manual compact is issued) → `failure_class: lock_contended` → more dead turns, until the compression finally commits.

### Observed timeline (one incident, single session, timestamps local; session id redacted)

```
15:40:09 conversation_loop: Pre-API compression: ~234,302 request tokens >= 231,200 threshold (context=272,000, attempt=1/3)
15:40:09 conversation_compression: context compression started: messages=193 tokens=~234,302
15:40:23 compression_attempt telemetry: commit_status=aborted failure_class=explicit_interrupt total_duration_ms=14230
15:40:23 turn_context: Preflight compression: ~240,941 tokens >= 231,200 threshold
15:40:23 conversation_compression: context compression started: messages=195 tokens=~240,941
15:41:14 run_agent: Session DB append_message failed: Session '<session>' is being compressed by another writer
15:41:14 conversation_compression: compression skipped: another path is compressing (failure_class=lock_contended)
15:42:00 run_agent: Session DB append_message failed: Session '<session>' is being compressed by another writer
15:42:05 run_agent: Session DB append_message failed: Session '<session>' is being compressed by another writer
15:42:05 conversation_loop: Turn ended: reason=session_persistence_failed api_calls=1/500 tool_turns=63 response_len=0
15:42:23 conversation_compression: Context compression still streaming after 120s (last progress 1.3s ago) — extending wait (ceiling 600s)
15:42:32 conversation_compression: context compression done: messages=195->90 rough_tokens=~111,084
15:42:32 compression_attempt telemetry: commit_status=committed total_duration_ms=129171
```

Eight minutes later the session crossed the threshold again and the same thing repeated — three more appends failed at 15:50:43, 15:50:48, 15:52:17–15:52:31, two more turns destroyed, plus a *manual* compact rejected with `failure_class=lock_contended`, before the second compression committed (`total_duration_ms=148096`, 173→97 messages). Note the second incident straddles a mid-session model switch, so the 5s wait also isn't something a user can dodge by changing models mid-flight.

The `compression_locks` row for these holds carried a **7-minute TTL** (`expires_at` = acquired + 420s), consistent with the 600s streaming ceiling — so the lock design already anticipates multi-minute compressions; only the busy-wait budget doesn't.

### Why the 5s budget can't just be raised naively

Per the #75264 review discussion, the lease is a correctness boundary (`test_compression_lease_blocks_non_owner_but_allows_owner_flush`): a writer that waits longer than the lease TTL could land a stale turn into a session whose compression is wedged. So the fix probably isn't `_COMPRESSION_BUSY_WAIT_S = 300`.

### Suggested directions

1. **Wait on the lock's own `expires_at`** (bounded by the remaining lease TTL, not a fixed 5s), rather than a constant that's an order of magnitude smaller than a healthy compression's duration. The lock row already carries `expires_at`; a waiter that outlives the *lease* can still be refused.
2. **Queue/spool the append instead of destroying the turn** — #74619 (lossless fallback spool + idempotent replay) would solve this class outright; linking it here as the durable fix.
3. **Fix the user-facing mapping**: `SessionCompressionInProgressError` should surface as "session is compacting — retrying/try again shortly", never as the "Disk full" dialog. Related: #74568 covers the same misleading surfacing for the stale-lock case.
4. Optionally: after a compression commits, add hysteresis so the post-compression token count sits well below the trigger threshold (both incidents re-triggered because the session hovered a few hundred tokens above it).

### Related

- #75083 (closed) — original report; fixed for short lock holds only
- #75264 — the 5s busy-wait fix this report follows up on
- #75316 — compression holding the session DB lock during API calls
- #74568 — stale-lock variant of the misleading disk/permission surfacing
- #74619 — RFC that would make this failure mode non-lossy

items.title: Buzz adapter: local image attachments always fail — send_image_file not overridden
items.body:
# Draft upstream issue — NousResearch/hermes-agent

**Title:** Buzz adapter: local image attachments always fail — `send_image_file` not overridden

**Labels:** bug, platform:buzz

---

### Summary

The Buzz platform adapter does not override `send_image_file`, so every local-file
image send falls through to the base-class stub and posts
`⚠️ Couldn't deliver the image attachment.` into the channel instead of the image.

This is surprising because the adapter **already has working local-file upload code**
in `send_image` — only the dispatch entry point is missing.

### Environment

- Hermes Agent v0.19.1
- Image `nousresearch/hermes-agent:v2026.7.30` (digest `sha256:b869e64d…`)
- Buzz relay `ghcr.io/block/buzz:sha-3e48f1b` (v0.5.2), self-hosted
- Buzz Desktop v0.5.3
- Platform: `gateway.platforms.buzz`, transport `websocket`

### Reproduce

1. Configure a Hermes profile with the Buzz gateway platform enabled.
2. Ask the agent to produce an image (e.g. a generated UI sketch) and send it to a channel.
3. Channel receives `⚠️ Couldn't deliver the image attachment.` — usually twice — and no image.

### Root cause

`gateway/platforms/base.py` `send_images()` dispatches by URI scheme:

- `file://` → `send_image_file()`
- `http(s)://` → `send_image()`

`plugins/platforms/buzz/adapter.py` implements `send_image` (line ~643) — whose own
docstring reads *"Send an image: local files upload via --file, URLs go as a link"* —
and it correctly builds:

    messages send --channel <id> --file <local> --content -

But `send_image_file` is never overridden, so local paths hit the base fallback at
`gateway/platforms/base.py:4309`:

    text = "⚠️ Couldn't deliver the image attachment."

Verified absent in both images checked:

    $ grep -c "async def send_image_file" /opt/hermes/plugins/platforms/buzz/adapter.py
    0     # v2026.7.30 (running)
    0     # :latest (2026-07-30T20:30)

### Suggested fix

Delegate to the existing, already-working method:

```python
async def send_image_file(
    self,
    chat_id: str,
    image_path: str,
    caption: Optional[str] = None,
    reply_to: Optional[str] = None,
    metadata: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None,
    **kwargs,
) -> SendResult:
    """Local-file image send — buzz CLI uploads via --file."""
    return await self.send_image(
        chat_id=chat_id,
        image_url=str(image_path),
        caption=caption,
        reply_to=reply_to,
        metadata=metadata,
    )
```

### Related

Same class of gap tracked for other adapters:
- #17261 — native `send_message` media delivery limited to Telegram, Discord, Matrix,
  WeChat, Signal (Buzz and Slack excluded)
- #5105 — Signal `MEDIA:` tags not extracted
- #6249 — Telegram echoes local path instead of uploading

### Docs mismatch

The Buzz adapter docs state *"Images are delivered as uploads (local files) or links
(URLs)"*, which does not currently hold for the local-file path.

### Note

There is no user-side workaround: the `buzz` CLI authenticates only via
`BUZZ_PRIVATE_KEY` / `--private-key` and does not read `BUZZ_CREDENTIALS_FILE`, so an
agent cannot upload the file itself from its shell and link the result.

items.title: Hermes Update issues.

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
# hermes update reliability — three related issues from a single update session

**Environment:** WSL2 (Ubuntu) on Windows, Lenovo LOQ, RTX 5060, hermes-agent 0.19.0 → 0.19.1
**Context:** All three surfaced during one `hermes update` run, and issue #2 has now recurred across two separate updates (2026-07-26 and 2026-08-03).

---

## 1. npm engines constraint isn't pre-flight-checked before pulling

`hermes update` pulls new code and only discovers an incompatible npm version during `npm install`, deep into the process — after Python deps are already updated and the repo is in a mixed state. The failure surfaces as a raw EBADENGINE stack trace with no guidance on what to do.

**Steps to reproduce**
1. Have npm <11.17.0 (but not in the excluded <11.10.0 range) installed
2. Run `hermes update` against a version of hermes-agent whose package.json requires `"npm": "<11.10.0 || >=11.17.0"`
3. Observe: code and Python deps update successfully, then Node dependency install fails with EBADENGINE, web UI build fails, desktop build fails — all cascading from the same root cause

**Expected behavior**
Before pulling changes (or immediately after, before attempting npm install), `hermes update` should compare the incoming package.json engines field against the currently installed npm/node versions and either:
- auto-offer to bump npm via `npm install -g npm@<required-version>`, or
- fail fast with a clear message: "This update requires npm >=11.17.0, you have 11.16.0. Run: npm install -g npm@11.17.0"

**Actual behavior**
Update proceeds, partially completes, leaves dashboard/TUI in a "mixed state" warning, and the user has to manually parse npm's raw error output to identify the fix.

**Repro environment**
Node v24.18.0, npm 11.16.0 (pre-fix)

---

## 2. Auto-stash mechanism repeatedly conflicts on package.json / package-lock.json

`hermes update` auto-stashes local changes before pulling, then attempts to restore them, which conflicts almost every update because root `package.json` mixes upstream-managed fields (deps, scripts) with a security-relevant allowlist (`allowScripts`) that legitimately gets modified both by users and by upstream in the same file. This has happened on two consecutive updates, each leaving an unresolved stash behind that the user has to manually diff and decide whether to drop.

**Steps to reproduce**
1. Run `hermes update` twice, a few weeks apart, on a repo with any local package.json state (even innocuous ones)
2. Observe the auto-stash → restore → `CONFLICT (content): Merge conflict in package.json / package-lock.json` pattern both times
3. Note the stash is left dangling with no follow-up guidance beyond "Restore your changes later with: git stash apply <ref>"

**Expected behavior**
Either:
- `allowScripts` (or any user-configurable security allowlist) should live in a separate, non-upstream-tracked file (e.g. `.hermes-allow-scripts.json`) that the updater never touches, or
- the updater should auto-diff the stash against the post-update file and auto-resolve when the only differences are upstream-generated lockfile noise (e.g. `"peer": true` toggles), only surfacing genuinely conflicting content to the user
- at minimum, `hermes update` should print a one-line summary of what's in the stash and whether it looks safe to drop, rather than leaving the user to run `git stash show -p` and interpret a raw diff

**Actual behavior**
User has to manually run git plumbing commands (`git stash show -p`, `git diff stash@{n}^..stash@{n}`) and cross-reference against HEAD to determine whether dropping the stash is safe.

**Recurrence**
2026-07-26 and 2026-08-03, same pattern both times.

---

## 3. Resolved package "downgrades" from exclude-newer policy aren't explained in update output

When `uv`'s `exclude-newer = "14 days"` policy (added in `pyproject.toml`, commit `88aed1b7`) causes the resolver to select an older package version than what was previously installed, `hermes update`'s output shows this as a bare version change with no context:

```
- cryptography==49.0.0
+ cryptography==48.0.1
- mcp==2.0.0
+ mcp==1.28.1
- uvicorn==0.52.0
+ uvicorn==0.41.0
```

This is visually indistinguishable from a genuine dependency pin reversion (a known separate class of issue where manually-pinned versions get silently dropped across updates), causing users to spend time investigating a non-issue.

**Steps to reproduce**
1. Run `hermes update` shortly after a dependency has a new release within the last 14 days
2. Observe the resolver silently selects the next-older version with no annotation
3. Compare against `git log -- pyproject.toml` to discover the actual cause (exclude-newer policy) — not discoverable from the update output itself

**Expected behavior**
When `exclude-newer` (or `exclude-newer-package` overrides) causes a resolution to differ from what a plain "latest" resolve would pick, `hermes update` should annotate the diff, e.g.:

```
~ cryptography 49.0.0 → 48.0.1 (held back: published <14 days ago, per exclude-newer policy)
```

**Actual behavior**
No indication given; the change is presented identically to an uncontrolled/accidental downgrade.

**Confirmed via**
`git show 88aed1b7 -- uv.lock pyproject.toml`

items.title: Update aborted by a non-Hermes python -m http.server process inside the install dir; dialog gives misleading 'Close other Hermes windows' advice

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Title
Update aborted by a non-Hermes `python -m http.server` process inside the install dir; dialog gives misleading "Close other Hermes windows" advice

## Body
### Summary
On Windows, the in-app / desktop "Update" aborts with:
```
Update aborted: another Hermes process is using this installation.

Close other Hermes windows and terminals, then retry. If the problem
persists, run `hermes update` in a terminal for detailed diagnostics.
```
In a real case the **only** blocker was a **stray `python -m http.server 8077`**
process that a user had started by hand to preview a local website, whose
working directory / process path lives under the Hermes install dir
(`%LOCALAPPDATA%\hermes\hermes-agent`). It is **not** a Hermes process, but the
blocker probe flags any `python.exe` under the install dir and aborts the update.

The advice in the dialog ("Close other Hermes windows and terminals") is then
**wrong and unactionable**: there are no Hermes windows/terminals to close, so
retry can never succeed through the UI.

This is distinct from the already-filed gateway-self-lock issues (#77277, #75334,
#70337): those are about Hermes-owned gateway/backend processes. Here the blocker
is a **user-launched, non-Hermes** process, and the failure mode is the
**misleading instruction**, not just a lock.

### Environment
- Windows 10
- Hermes Desktop (Electron), install at `C:\Users\<user>\AppData\Local\hermes\hermes-agent` (git checkout, main)
- Hermes Agent v0.19.1

### Steps to Reproduce
1. From a terminal, `cd` into any dir and run `python -m http.server 8077` (or start a preview server that ends up with a process path under the Hermes install dir), leaving it running in the background.
2. Open Hermes Desktop and click the in-app **Update** button.
3. Observe: `Update aborted: another Hermes process is using this installation` — even with no Hermes windows or terminals open.
4. Click **Retry** — fails identically. The `http.server` process is never mentioned.

### Expected Behavior
- The blocker probe should distinguish **Hermes-owned** processes (gateway, serve, backend) from **arbitrary third-party `python.exe`** living under the install dir.
- If a non-Hermes process is the blocker, the message should name it explicitly, e.g.:
  > Update aborted: port 8077 is held by `python -m http.server` (PID 21544), which is not a Hermes process. Close or stop that process, then retry.
- The generic "Close other Hermes windows and terminals" text should only appear when the blocker is actually a Hermes-owned window/terminal.

### Impact
Users who run local dev servers / preview servers (common with `python -m http.server`) inside or near the Hermes install dir hit a dead-end loop through the Desktop UI and can only recover by running `hermes update` in a terminal (which kills the session as a side effect) or by manually hunting the PID. The misleading instruction makes the cause non-obvious.

### Suggested Fix
In the venv-blocker scan (`apps/desktop/electron/venv-blocker-scan.ts` or equivalent):
- Classify each candidate process as `hermes-owned` vs `foreign` (e.g. command line contains `hermes_cli.main` / known service args vs anything else).
- For `foreign` blockers, report the exact command line + PID + port so the user can stop the right process.
- Only show the "Close other Hermes windows/terminals" guidance when the blocker set is non-empty AND consists solely of Hermes-owned UI/terminal processes.

items.title: fix(security): emission gaps — process(list) raw, traceback in tool result, *_KEY regex miss, control-char split, ACP plain formatter

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Severity: MEDIUM (Agent 6-restart F1-F5).

- `process(action=list)` returns raw `command[:200]` + raw `output_buffer[-200:]` with NO redaction wrap (process_registry.py:2486-2496, 1863/1869) — poll/log/wait/kill are all redacted; list isn't; raw command also persisted to the checkpoint file (2066-2068).
- The terminal_tool exception path returns raw `traceback.format_exc()` + raw `str(e)` (terminal_tool.py:3149-3161) — only the logger.error copy is redacted.
- `_ENV_ASSIGN_RE` misses `*_KEY`/`*_PASS`/`*_PW` (redact.py:136-139) — VERIFIED LIVE: FAL_KEY/OPENAI_KEY/MYSQL_PASS/DB_PW pass unmasked.
- Tokens split by `\r`/`\n`/ESC/zero-width chars escape every regex (redact.py:437-439, verified).
- The ACP adapter clears root handlers and installs a PLAIN logging.Formatter — zero redaction in that process (acp_adapter/entry.py:81-95, 236).

Fix: redact process(list) + exception paths; extend the env-name regex; normalize control chars before matching; use RedactingFormatter in ACP.

items.title: [Bug]: gateway routing index is fully rewritten with fsync 2-3 times per user message for one entry's metadata bump

labels.name: sweeper:risk-session-state
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may lose/corrupt/mis-associate session or context state

items.body:
### Bug Description

Every healthy inbound gateway message and every turn end persists the session routing index by rewriting the whole thing: serialize every entry, delete all rows for the scope, insert all of them back, and rewrite the full `sessions.json` mirror with `indent` + `fsync`. This happens 2-3 times per user message.

Two trigger points in `gateway/session.py`:

1. The per-message healthy path (`session.py:2397`): `entry.updated_at = now` flags `_needs_save`, which runs `_save_entries()` (`session.py:2464`).
2. `update_session` at turn end (`session.py:2507`): calls `_save()` while holding the global session `_lock`, so one session's fsync blocks all concurrent routing.

Both go through `replace_gateway_routing_entries` (`hermes_state.py:3062`), which is `DELETE FROM gateway_routing WHERE scope = ?` + `executemany(INSERT)` of every entry, plus the mirror rewrite (`session.py:1498-1536`).

The cost is O(S) writes + a full-file fsync per message, where S is every routing entry the gateway has ever kept (bounded only by the 90-day prune). The actual change being persisted is one entry's `updated_at` or `last_prompt_tokens`.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Instrument `SessionDB.replace_gateway_routing_entries` and `save_gateway_routing_entry` with call counters on a running gateway (or a store-level test).
2. Send 2 messages to an existing gateway session.
3. Observe 2-3 full-index rewrites (each O(S) row writes + mirror fsync) and zero single-key upserts, even though only one entry's metadata changed.

### Expected Behavior

Metadata-only bumps persist as a single-key upsert (the `save_gateway_routing_entry` upsert already exists at `hermes_state.py:3034` for exactly this shape). Whole-index rewrites happen on structural changes (new/reset/pruned entries), and no save runs while holding the global session lock.

### Actual Behavior

Every user message triggers 2-3 whole-index rewrites + fsync, one of them under the global lock.

### Affected Component

Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp

### Debug Report

```shell
Not a runtime crash. Per-message write amplification in
gateway/session.py routing persistence.
```

### Operating System

Windows 11

### Python Version

3.13.13

### Hermes Version

main @ d79a6f0e3 (0.19.1)

### Additional Logs / Traceback (optional)

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

`gateway/session.py:2397-2398` and `session.py:2507-2515` route every save through the whole-index writer. The delete-all + insert-all semantics exist so pruned/reset sessions disappear from the index atomically (documented on `replace_gateway_routing_entries`), which is only needed on structural changes. The `sessions.json` mirror is a legacy fallback; its readers (`channel_directory.py:375-433`, downgrade routing) consume origin and session_id fields, which only change structurally, so mirror rewrites are not needed for metadata bumps either.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

Metadata-only bumps (updated_at, last_prompt_tokens) persist via the existing single-key upsert, sharing the generation guard with the whole-index writer so a stale delayed full replace cannot clobber a newer upsert. Structural changes keep the full replace + mirror rewrite. `update_session` persists outside the global lock. PR ready.

### Are you willing to submit a PR for this?

- [x] I'd like to fix this myself and submit a PR

items.title: save_config() overwrites custom provider config with DEFAULT_CONFIG values on every runtime trigger

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Bug: `save_config()` overwrites custom provider config with DEFAULT_CONFIG values on every runtime trigger

### Environment
- **Hermes Agent:** v0.19.1 (2026.7.30), git install
- **OS:** Ubuntu 25.10 (Linux 7.0.0-28-generic x86_64)
- **Python:** 3.11.15
- **Platform:** Telegram gateway (systemd)

### Description

When using a **custom OpenAI-compatible provider** (`custom_providers` with custom `base_url` and `api_key`), the `config.yaml` is silently overwritten at runtime — replacing the user's model, API key, and provider with `DEFAULT_CONFIG` values. This happens without any user action.

**User's config (minimal, valid):**
```yaml
model:
  context_length: 1000000
  default: ag/claude-opus-4-6-thinking
  provider: custom:myrouter
custom_providers:
  - api_key: sk-user-key-here
    base_url: http://my-server:1997/v1
    model: ag/claude-opus-4-6-thinking
    name: myrouter
_config_version: 33
```

**After runtime overwrite, config becomes:**
```yaml
model:
  default: ag/gemini-3-flash-agent    # ← CHANGED to default
providers:
  custom:myrouter:
    api_key: sk-different-key          # ← CHANGED
    api_mode: openai
    base_url: http://my-server:1997/v1
agent:
  max_turns: 150                       # ← INJECTED from DEFAULT_CONFIG
  restart_drain_timeout: 180
  verify_on_stop: false
  # ... 50+ more default keys injected
compression:
  hygiene_hard_message_limit: 400      # ← INJECTED
# ... full DEFAULT_CONFIG dump
# ── Security ─────────────────────────
# ... commented template appended
# ── Fallback Model ───────────────────
# ... commented template appended
```

The user's chosen model (`claude-opus-4-6-thinking`) and API key are replaced with defaults, breaking the connection to their custom provider. **The agent becomes unusable until the user manually restores config.yaml.**

### Root Cause

`save_config()` in `hermes_cli/config.py` (line ~3505):

1. Calls `load_config()` which **deep-merges** user config with `DEFAULT_CONFIG`
2. The merged result treats DEFAULT_CONFIG values as authoritative — user's `model.default` and `api_key` are overwritten
3. Writes the **full merged dict** back to disk, including all default keys the user never set
4. Appends commented Security and Fallback Model templates

This function is triggered at runtime by at least 3 code paths **without any user action:**

| Trigger | Location | When |
|---|---|---|
| `persist_home_channel()` | `gateway/config.py:482` | Gateway detects Telegram home channel |
| `monitoring install_id` | `agent/monitoring/policy.py:44` | Every gateway start (if no install_id) |
| `migrate_config()` | `hermes_cli/config.py:2367` | Gateway start (if `_config_version` < latest) |

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure a custom OpenAI-compatible provider in `config.yaml` with a non-default model
2. Set `_config_version` to any value lower than the current `DEFAULT_CONFIG` version (or let any of the 3 triggers fire)
3. Start/restart the gateway (`hermes gateway run`)
4. `cat ~/.hermes/config.yaml` — observe that model, API key, and provider have been replaced with defaults, and 50+ default keys have been injected

### Related Prior Fixes (incomplete)

This bug class has been partially addressed before, but the runtime triggers above still cause it:

- `89d812777` — "fix: setup wizard overwrites custom endpoint config (#4172)" — same symptom, different trigger
- `c717be8de` — "fix(config): route every migration write through one default-stripping chokepoint" — commit message explicitly mentions user reports: *"you blow up my profile config on one tweak"*
- `123c6f3a2` — "fix(config): close unreadable-overwrite bug class at a single chokepoint" — identified 7+ independent write sites

### Expected Behavior

- `save_config()` should **never overwrite** user-set values (`model.default`, `api_key`, `provider`) with DEFAULT_CONFIG defaults
- Runtime triggers that only need to persist a single key (e.g., `install_id`, `home_channel`) should use a surgical write, not a full config dump
- Custom provider configurations should survive gateway restarts

### Current Workaround

Running a real-time `inotifywait` watchdog (via PM2) that detects any change to `config.yaml` and restores from a known-good backup within <1 second. This is a band-aid, not a fix.

### Impact

- **Severity:** High — renders the agent completely unusable (wrong model, wrong API key, can't connect)
- **Frequency:** Every gateway restart or Telegram home channel detection
- **User action required:** None — happens silently in the background
- **Affected users:** Anyone using `custom_providers` with a non-default model

items.title: [Bug] T9 (九方) IME: typing creates new session automatically

labels.name: sweeper:risk-platform-windows
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break or behave differently on native Windows

items.body:
## Bug Description

When using the **T9 (九方) Chinese input method** (q922b5.exe) to type in the Hermes Desktop chat composer, each character selected from the T9 candidate list causes the app to automatically jump to a **new session** — instead of simply inserting the character into the current chat.

This makes the T9 input method completely unusable with Hermes Desktop.

## Environment

| Item | Value |
|------|-------|
| **Hermes Version** | v0.19.1 (2026.7.30) |
| **Platform** | Windows 11 (Desktop app) |
| **IME** | 九方 T9 (q922b5.exe) |
| **IME NOT affected** | Standard Microsoft Pinyin works correctly |

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Open Hermes Desktop app
2. Focus on the chat composer input
3. Switch to T9 (九方) input method
4. Type strokes using number keys (e.g., press keys to form a character)
5. Select a character from the T9 candidate list
6. **Expected**: The character is inserted into the composer, user continues typing
7. **Actual**: A new session is created immediately, character is lost or placed in the wrong session

## Root Cause Analysis

The T9 IME (q922b5.exe) uses window classes `qcIME` (candidate window) and `q92k2panelb5` (panel). Unlike standard CJK IMEs (Pinyin, Bopomofo), T9 may not properly trigger `compositionstart`/`compositionend` DOM events, or may use `SendInput` with `KEYEVENTF_UNICODE` to insert characters — bypassing the normal IME composition flow.

The Hermes composer relies on `composingRef` (set by `compositionstart`/`compositionend`) and `event.nativeEvent.isComposing` to detect active IME composition. When T9 doesn't trigger these events, the character insertion may be misinterpreted as a keyboard shortcut or trigger an unintended action.

## What I Tried

1. **Python WH_KEYBOARD_LL hook** to suppress Enter during T9 composition — hook installed but never received any events (MSYS bash environment issue)
2. **PowerShell Start-Process** to launch hook in native Windows context — same result
3. **VBS launcher** for proper Windows console — hook still received no events
4. **Window monitoring** to detect T9 candidate window (`qcIME` class) — detection worked, but could not intercept the actual key events

## Additional Context

- The existing issue #54144 covers Chinese IME Enter submitting during composition (macOS-focused)
- This T9-specific issue is different: the new session is created **during character selection**, not just on Enter press
- T9 input method is commonly used in Hong Kong and is not replaceable for users who rely on it
- The T9 IME process (q922b5.exe, PID varies) runs as a separate process with its own windows

## Suggestion

The composer should track composition state more robustly — possibly by monitoring the T9 IME window visibility (`qcIME` class) rather than relying solely on DOM `compositionstart`/`compositionend` events, since T9 may not fire these standard events.

items.title: [Bug]: Desktop SSH serve inherits macOS 256-FD limit with no YAML override

labels.name: sweeper:risk-compatibility
labels.description: Sweeper risk: may break existing users, config, migrations, defaults, or upgrades

items.body:
## Bug description

On macOS, Hermes Desktop's SSH backend launches `hermes serve --isolated` with the inherited `RLIMIT_NOFILE` soft limit of 256. Unlike launchd-managed gateway work, the Desktop SSH launch path has no resource-limit floor and Hermes exposes no `config.yaml` setting for it.

A long-lived isolated backend can therefore hit `EMFILE` with only a few visible agents. Once exhausted, unrelated subsystems fail together because the next innocent `open()` or socket allocation crosses the process limit.

Observed cascade:

```text
agent init failed: [Errno 24] Too many open files: '<profile>/auth.lock'
resume failed: handler error: unable to open database file
api keys failed to load: socket hangup
```

Settings/providers and session lists then appear blank even though auth and `state.db` remain intact.

## Steps to reproduce

1. On macOS, confirm the inherited soft limit:

   ```sh
   launchctl limit maxfiles
   python3 -c 'import resource; print(resource.getrlimit(resource.RLIMIT_NOFILE))'
   ```

   Observed: `256 / unlimited`.

2. Connect Hermes Desktop to the Mac over SSH. Desktop constructs the remote launch in `apps/desktop/electron/remote-lifecycle.ts::buildSpawnCommand()`:

   ```text
   env HERMES_DESKTOP=1 <hermes> ... serve --isolated ...
   ```

3. Keep that isolated backend alive while sessions/delegation create short-lived SQLite readers or other FD-bearing resources.
4. Inspect the backend with `lsof -n -P -a -p <pid>`.

Incident evidence from a single backend:

```text
RLIMIT_NOFILE soft: 256
regular-file handles: 225
state.db handles: 106
state.db-wal handles: 102
```

Only a few logical agents were active. `state.db` passed `PRAGMA quick_check`, and auth inventory remained valid after the backend was restarted with headroom.

A shell child can raise itself without root because the hard limit permits it:

```text
child before: 256
child after: 4096
```

## Expected behavior

Long-lived Hermes server surfaces should best-effort raise their `RLIMIT_NOFILE` soft limit to a safe configurable floor before opening databases, sockets, MCP transports, or agent resources.

A non-secret `config.yaml` option should:

- default to a conservative value such as 4096;
- use `0`/`null` to disable;
- never lower an already-higher soft limit;
- clamp to the OS hard limit;
- fail open on Windows, unsupported platforms, and restricted environments.

Both `hermes gateway run` and `hermes serve --isolated` should use one shared implementation.

## Actual behavior

Current main has no `RLIMIT_NOFILE` startup helper or YAML option. Desktop's SSH backend inherits 256 unchanged.

## Root cause analysis

`apps/desktop/electron/remote-lifecycle.ts::buildSpawnCommand()` detaches a shell that directly executes `hermes serve --isolated`. Resource limits are inherited across SSH, shell, detach, and exec. Reparenting the detached process does not recalculate them.

This is a capacity/failure-containment gap, separate from individual FD lifecycle bugs. In this incident, SessionDB reader retention is tracked by #75269 / #75322, but raising the process floor remains useful defense-in-depth and prevents one modest leak or legitimate multi-agent workload from immediately disabling auth, sessions, providers, and sockets together.

## Prior art and boundary

- #30230 reports the same macOS 256 limit for gateways.
- #30234 proposed a gateway-only `_raise_fd_soft_limit(4096)` helper but was closed unmerged to reduce queue pressure.
- #50494 adds launchd plist limits and Telegram pool fixes; it does not cover SSH-spawned `serve --isolated` or YAML configuration.
- #75269 / #75322 address the SessionDB reader lifecycle root cause and should remain a separate, complementary change.

A clean fix should centralize #30234's sound limit/clamp behavior, use the real config loader and direct tests, and wire both long-lived Python entry points without absorbing the SQLite or Telegram/launchd patches.

## Environment

- macOS 26.5
- Python 3.11.15
- Hermes Agent v0.19.1
- current-main reproduction reviewed at `536ed6a33e4c46fc7d258d8181ad250c2bc404a3`

## PR

A focused current-main PR with configuration, shared runtime helper, startup wiring, tests, and docs will follow.

items.title: [Feature] Gateway-owned owner-loop job dispatcher with cancellation/drain acknowledgements

labels.name: needs-decision
labels.description: Awaiting maintainer decision before any implementation

items.body:
## Problem

A plugin/tool handler may execute on a non-Gateway asyncio loop while it must call connected platform adapters owned by `GatewayRunner._gateway_loop`. Today the only available integration is a private raw loop handle plus `asyncio.run_coroutine_threadsafe()`.

That boundary cannot provide safe cancellation/shutdown semantics. Deterministic real-loop probes reproduced:

- a caller receives timeout/cancellation, then the owner task begins effects afterwards;
- stop-after-submission leaves an unawaited coroutine and a destroyed pending Task;
- plugin-submitted work is not part of Gateway shutdown drain because it is absent from Gateway-owned background-task lifecycle.

This blocks a production Current Work plugin from proving that no SQLite/platform effect can happen after a terminal tool result.

Related consumer issue: Codier/WaterOS#58.

## Required public contract

Expose a Gateway-owned, thread-safe owner-job API, conceptually:

```python
handle = gateway.submit_owner_job(factory)
await handle.result()
await handle.cancel_and_wait()
```

`factory` must be invoked only after owner-loop admission; callers must never pass a pre-created coroutine.

The Gateway owns a serialized state machine:

```text
PENDING -> CLAIMED -> RUNNING -> TERMINAL
        -> CANCELLED
        -> STOPPED
```

Required semantics:

1. Pre-claim cancellation atomically removes/marks the request; any later owner callback is a no-op and never invokes `factory`.
2. Post-claim cancellation returns only after the Gateway cancels/drains the tracked task and publishes terminal cleanup acknowledgement.
3. Gateway shutdown first enters `CLOSING`, rejects/drains pending requests, cancels and awaits claimed tasks/finalizers, then disconnects adapters/closes the loop.
4. Every accepted handle reaches one terminal result. No caller-visible timeout/cancellation may be followed by later job effects.
5. The API must preserve genuine caller cancellation while still completing owner-side cleanup.
6. Plugins must not access `_gateway_loop` or `_background_tasks` directly.

## Acceptance tests

Use real independent asyncio loops and fail on `RuntimeWarning` or destroyed pending Tasks:

- pre-claim caller cancellation;
- stop before owner callback;
- post-claim timeout/cancellation with cleanup acknowledgement;
- stop after claim;
- owner task exception and cancellation;
- loop close with pending and running jobs;
- same-loop submission without deadlock;
- exactly-once factory invocation;
- no effect after terminal result;
- bounded, privacy-normalized error surface for plugin callers.

## Non-goals

- No credential loading or platform-specific REST fallback.
- No plugin-owned shadow task registry.
- No arbitrary operation timeout for jobs that are already running normally.

items.title: Desktop: status bar hidden by default for new users - plugins, gateway status, command center and update notifications all invisible
items.body:
## Summary

Commit **`d399c1644`** ("fix(desktop): statusbar off by default", author Brooklyn Nicholson, 2026-07-31) made the status bar **opt-in**: on fresh installs and reinstalls the whole bar is not rendered at all. Because the bar hosts more than status readouts, this silently removes several features from new-user UIs:

1. **Desktop plugins become invisible.** Plugins (UI extensions registered into `statusBar.right`) depend on the bar to render. With the bar hidden, a correctly installed and enabled plugin appears as if it were never installed. New users assume it is a bug in the plugin; users who reinstall also spend a long time troubleshooting before discovering the bar is simply off by default.
2. **The bottom-left command center becomes unreachable.** The command entries (sessions / system / usage / maintenance) live on the status bar; hiding it removes all those quick actions.
3. **Gateway connection status is no longer visible.** The bar carries the gateway/connection indicator, so users cannot tell whether the AI backend is connected.
4. **The version update notification disappears.** The bottom-right update notice is gone together with the bar, so users cannot discover new releases in time.

## Steps to reproduce

1. Fresh install (or reinstall) Hermes Desktop 0.19.1 (includes `d399c1644`).
2. Enable any desktop plugin (drop it into `<hermes-home>/plugins` or run `hermes plugins enable`).
3. Launch Hermes — the bottom status bar is not rendered, so the plugin chip, gateway status, command center and update notice are all invisible.
4. Press Ctrl+K and type "status bar" to turn the bar on manually — everything works again.

## Expected behavior

- The status bar should be **visible by default**;
- Users can still hide it via `view.toggleStatusbar` and that choice persists.

## Environment

- Hermes 0.19.1 (Desktop)
- Windows x64

Attachment: an example desktop plugin (`deepseek-balance.zip`, registers into `statusBar.right`) is attached to reproduce the issue.

---

# 中文翻译

## 摘要

官方提交 **`d399c1644`** —— `fix(desktop): statusbar off by default`（作者 Brooklyn Nicholson，2026-07-31）—— 将状态栏改为 **opt-in**：全新安装或重装后，整条状态栏完全不渲染。由于状态栏承载的不只是状态读数，这一改动让新用户界面上的多项功能"静默消失"：

1. **桌面插件不可见**：插件（注册在 `statusBar.right` 区域的 UI 扩展）依赖状态栏渲染。状态栏隐藏后，正确安装且已启用的插件看起来像从未安装过。新用户会误以为是插件 bug；重装用户也会花很长时间排查，最后才发现只是状态栏默认关闭。
2. **左下角命令中心无法使用**：会话 / 系统 / 用量 / 维护等命令入口都挂在状态栏上，隐藏后这些快捷操作全部不可达。
3. **网关连接状态不可见**：状态栏承载了网关/连接状态指示，隐藏后用户无法确认是否已连接 AI。
4. **版本更新提示消失**：右下角的更新提示随状态栏一起消失，用户无法及时获知新版本。

## 复现步骤

1. 全新安装（或重新安装）Hermes Desktop 0.19.1（包含 `d399c1644`）。
2. 启用任意桌面插件（放入 `<hermes-home>/plugins` 或运行 `hermes plugins enable`）。
3. 启动 Hermes —— 底部状态栏不渲染，插件芯片、网关状态、命令中心、更新提示全部不可见。
4. 按 Ctrl+K 输入 "status bar" 手动开启状态栏后，一切恢复正常。

## 期望行为

- 状态栏**默认可见**；
- 用户仍可通过 `view.toggleStatusbar` 自行隐藏，且选择会持久保存。

## 环境

- Hermes 0.19.1 (Desktop)
- Windows x64

附件：附上一个示例桌面插件（`deepseek-balance.zip`，注册在 `statusBar.right` 区域），可复现上述问题。

[deepseek-balance.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/30659221/deepseek-balance.zip)
